newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Power rests with Karadzic in Bosnian Serb feud.
newsitem.headline: Power rests with Karadzic in Bosnian Serb feud.

text.p: Indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic is out to prove once again that only he and his hardline allies call the shots in Bosnian Serb territory.
Karadzic loyalists detained Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic at the weekend after she dared blow the whistle on high-level corruption and war profiteering.
Plavsic kept up her outspoken criticism after she was released on Monday, but Karadzic's circle holds all the important levers of power, controlling the media, the police and state-run monopolies.
The hardliners who orchestrated wartime "ethnic cleansing" of Bosnian Moslems and Croats as well as the brutal siege of Sarajevo have never shown charity to their political rivals.

They nominated Plavsic believing she would serve as an obedient successor to Karadzic, who was forced to step down from office under heavy international pressure last year because he had been indicted twice by the U.N. war crimes tribunal on former Yugoslavia.
Instead, Plavsic called for an investigation into alleged corruption linked to companies run by Karadzic and urged cooperation with Western powers offering postwar reconstruction aid.
When Plavsic called for the suspension of one of Karadzic's most loyal servants, Interior Minister Dragan Kijac, it was more than the leadership would tolerate.
"We have to say that the president of the Serb republic is deceiving the public," Serb television said in a sharp rebuke.
Plavsic tried to speak to a radio station in Banja Luka on Monday night, but the town's power supply went down.
"That was a clear message telling her they could put her in the dark any time they wanted," said one diplomat in Sarajevo.
While Plavsic complained to reporters on Tuesday of an "anti-democratic atmosphere", leaders of Karadzic's ruling party met in their headquarters in Pale, outside Sarajevo, to discuss her fate.
The Serb party officials arriving in Pale looked more confident and relaxed than Western envoys in Sarajevo.
Although Plavsic herself is a nationalist ideologue, U.S. and European states have tried to promote her as a more pragmatic alternative to Karadzic's circle.
The NATO-led peace force deployed extra troops to prevent any possible violence but it was unclear if Plavsic enjoyed the loyalty of a significant number of police or army officers.
Other Bosnian Serb politicians who have tried to strike out on their own and cooperate with Western governments have been crushed with ease.
Former prime minister Rajko Kasagic and the former mayor of Banja Luka, Predrag Rakic, were pushed out of the political arena for their disobedience.
United States special envoy Robert Gelbard was careful not to openly side with Plavsic when asked about the feud on Tuesday, calling for Serb authorities to abide by their constitution.
Western governments were waiting anxiously to see whether the ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS) would decide to remove Plavsic or merely strip her of real authority.
Diplomats said it was doubtful that the Serb republic's constitution allowed the president to be removed by a parliamentary vote.
Because Plavsic was elected president in an election paid for and blessed by the international community, her illegal removal would put major powers in an awkward position.
Karadzic always relished his defiance of Western powers when his army held the upper hand during the Bosnian war.
This week's crisis has shown that Karadzic remains a thorn in the side of American and European envoys struggling to shore up a fragile peace in Bosnia.
